full_judgment: In the reported case of course, the pre-emption case was under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act which was contested on the ground that the land purchased by the pre-emptees appertained to an under-raiyati holding created by registered kabuliyat dated 10th October, 1947 in favour of their vendor Moslemuddin; and as such the petitioner not being a co- sharer in the under-raiyati holding could not maintain the pre-emption case. Pre-emptor relied upon the doctrine of merger and upgradation of under raiyati on the elimination of the rent receiving interest over the vendor Moslemuddin. Pre-emption case was allowed by the trial Court and it was affirmed by the lower Appel1ate Court Opposite parties moved the High Court and rule was issued At the hearing of the rule it was argued that in view of the fact that all rent-receiving interests have been acquired by the Government on and from 14th April, 1956. Moslemuddin who was an under-raiyat, became a tenant direct under the Government and was therefore automatically elevated to the status of an occupancy raiyat, and that being the position in law Moslemuddin status in the under raiyati was upgraded, and consequently the petitioner became a co-sharer in the holding and therefore rightly claimed pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In answer to this contention it was argued that until final acquisition took place on the publication of tile compensation assessment roll under section 43(2) of the Act all rent-receiving interests no doubt vested in the Government but that was more or less a national vesting, because, until Part V came into operation and the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed, "One class of holders of agricultural land" that is, one class of tenants (Malik's) as provided in section 81 did not come into being. It was argued that the different' provisions of the statute show that even after the general notification of 2nd April. 1956 and the consequent, vesting of all rent receiving interests in the Government, the different classes of tenancies recognized under the Bengal Tenancy Act continued, because continuation of different classes of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act was necessary for the purpose of assessment of compensation and calculation of rate (If compensation to be paid to tenants of different classes. It was also submitted that after all these steps including the final publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll under section 43(2) of the Act, actual vesting of the different interests in the Government, as provided under section 44 of the Act, took place.
